paragraphs: In some places the custom is that the kohanim themselves begin the word "yevarechecha," and the chazzan (prayer leader) only calls out to them from the word "Hashem veyishmerecha" onward, and this is the reasoning that Maran [Rabbi Yosef Karo] wrote of blessed memory in his pure Shulchan Aruch. But some say that the chazzan must call out to them the word "yevarechecha" as well, because it is written "say to them," and there is a requirement in this matter; but those who disagree hold that there is no requirement if he did not say to them the word "yevarechecha." However, according to the esoteric tradition (Kabbalah) there is a requirement in this, to say to them the word "yevarechecha" as well, as Rabbeinu Bechaye of blessed memory wrote in Parashat Naso, explaining the reason why it is necessary to call out "yevarechecha" as well - see there. And so the chassidim of Beit El, may it be built and established, in Jerusalem practice. And behold, here in our city of Baghdad, may it be guarded, the custom from ancient times, as Maran of blessed memory wrote, was that the chazzan does not call out the word "yevarechecha." But some years ago, praised be the blessed God who helped me institute the practice in all the synagogues of our city that the chazzan should call out the word "yevarechecha" as well, and so it is fitting to instruct in every place. And this custom has benefited us greatly, for through it the congregation does not lose the "amen" that follows the blessing "Yisrael be'ahavah" (Israel, in love); for previously it was the way of the kohanim to hasten to say "yevarechecha" immediately after the word "be'ahavah" in one breath, and because of this it was not possible to answer amen.

clarification.explanation: Regarding Birkat Kohanim (the Priestly Blessing), customs differ as to how it begins. Some practice that the kohanim open the word "yevarechecha" on their own, and the chazzan calls out to them only from the words "Hashem veyishmerecha" onward - and this is the position of Maran in the Shulchan Aruch. But some say that the chazzan must call out to the kohanim the word "yevarechecha" as well, as it is said "say to them," and according to the esoteric tradition one must be careful to call out "yevarechecha" to them as well. In Baghdad the custom from earlier times followed Maran's view that the chazzan does not call out "yevarechecha," but our teacher [the Ben Ish Chai] changed the custom in all the synagogues of the city so that the chazzan would call out "yevarechecha" as well, and so it is fitting to instruct everywhere. This custom brings great benefit, for through it the congregation does not lose out on answering "amen" after the blessing "Yisrael be'ahavah," since previously the kohanim would hurry to say "yevarechecha" immediately after "be'ahavah" in a single breath, leaving the congregation no time to answer amen.
takeaways: Our teacher instituted that the chazzan calls out to the kohanim the word "yevarechecha" as well, and so it is fitting everywhere.
The benefit: the congregation has time to answer amen after the blessing "Yisrael be'ahavah."

paragraphs: If there are no kohanim to perform the raising of hands (nesiat kapayim), and the time is appropriate for the raising of hands, then the prayer leader says "Bless us with the blessing, etc." as mentioned in the prayer books, and the congregation does not answer amen after the verses, but says "May it be [His] will" after each verse. And it is written in Chesed LeAlafim: the custom of the early pious ones (vatikin) is to say after the first verse "May it be [His] will, in the merit of Abraham," and after the second verse "May it be [His] will, in the merit of Isaac," and after the third verse "May it be [His] will, in the merit of Jacob, and in the merit of Moses, Aaron, Joseph, and David."

clarification.explanation: If there are no kohanim for the raising of hands, and the time is appropriate for it, the prayer leader says "Bless us with the blessing," etc. (in the wording found in the prayer books), and the congregation does not answer "amen" after the verses, but says "May it be [His] will" after each verse. Chesed LeAlafim writes that the custom of the vatikin is to say after the first verse "May it be [His] will, in the merit of Abraham," after the second "in the merit of Isaac," and after the third "in the merit of Jacob, and in the merit of Moses, Aaron, Joseph, and David."
takeaways: When there are no kohanim, the prayer leader says "Bless us with the blessing," and the congregation answers "May it be [His] will" after each verse (not "amen").
The custom of the vatikin: "May it be [His] will, in the merit of Abraham/Isaac/Jacob and Moses, Aaron, Joseph, and David" after the verses.

paragraphs: When the prayer leader says "yevarechecha," [the kohanim] face toward the Ark (Heichal); "veyishmerecha" - toward the right side; "ya'er Hashem panav" - toward the Ark; "eilecha vichunecha" - toward the left side; so wrote Chesed LeAlafim. But the rabbi, his son, wrote there in the name of "Apei Zutrei," quoting from the letters of Rabbi Moshe Zacuto of blessed memory: "yevarechecha" - toward his right side; "ya'er" - toward the left; "yisa" - toward his face, and he wrote there that this is the plain custom in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be built and established, and so practice the congregation of the chassidim in Beit El, may it be guarded. And I asked our beloved friend, the great sage our teacher Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may his light shine, to inform me of the custom of the chassidim in Beit El, may it be guarded, in this matter, and he wrote to me, and these are his words: "Be it known that what 'Apei Zutrei' wrote in the name of the letters of Rabbi Moshe Zacuto of blessed memory has no proof; and I practice according to the language of the Zohar and as Chesed LeAlafim wrote, and not as the rabbi's son emended it, and the custom of Beit El, may it be guarded, is as I do; and see 'Tefilat Kol Peh' page 80, column 3, and see 'Kaf HaChaim' siman 15, letter 77, that the word 'yevarechecha, etc.' - toward the Ark; 'veyishmerecha' - toward the right; 'ya'er' - toward the Ark; 'eilecha veyachonecha' - toward the left; 'yisa' - opposite the Ark, and the middle line - which is his own body." Thus far his words, may his light shine.

clarification.explanation: To which side should the prayer leader turn during Birkat Kohanim? Opinions differ: According to Chesed LeAlafim - "yevarechecha" faces toward the Ark, "veyishmerecha" toward the right, "ya'er Hashem panav" toward the Ark, "eilecha vichunecha" toward the left. But his son quoted in the name of "Apei Zutrei" (from the letters of the Ramaz, of blessed memory): "yevarechecha" to his right, "ya'er" to his left, "yisa" toward his face - and wrote that this is the custom in Jerusalem and in Beit El. The Ben Ish Chai asked Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may his light shine, [about this], and he replied that there is no proof for the words of "Apei Zutrei," and that he practices according to the language of the Zohar and as Chesed LeAlafim wrote (and not as the son's emendation), and so is the custom of Beit El. See also Kaf HaChaim: "yevarechecha" toward the Ark, "veyishmerecha" to the right, "ya'er" toward the Ark, "eilecha vichunecha" to the left, "yisa" opposite the Ark, and the middle line - opposite his own body.
takeaways: The direction the prayer leader faces during Birkat Kohanim - a dispute between Chesed LeAlafim (following the language of the Zohar) and his son's emendation (in the name of the Ramaz).

In practice, following the language of the Zohar/Kaf HaChaim: "yevarechecha"/"ya'er"/"yisa" toward the Ark, "veyishmerecha" to the right, "eilecha vichunecha" to the left (and the middle facing his own body) - and so is the custom of Beit El.

paragraphs: Any kohen who has none of the disqualifying factors, if he does not go up to the duchan (platform), has nullified a positive commandment, and is considered to have transgressed three positive commandments if he was in the synagogue at the time the chazzan called "Kohanim," or if he was explicitly told to go up or to wash his hands. And every kohen who blesses is blessed from Above. And, praised be God, here in our city of Baghdad, may it be guarded, they are careful to perform the raising of hands every day, and so it is fitting to practice in all congregations, for through Birkat Kohanim abundance is drawn down to the upper and lower worlds, and there are in it secrets of secrets - fortunate is the eye that has seen it.

clarification.explanation: Any kohen who has no disqualifying factor preventing him from raising his hands, and who does not go up to the duchan, has nullified a positive commandment. And if he was in the synagogue at the time the chazzan called "Kohanim," or was explicitly told to go up or to wash his hands, he is considered to have transgressed three positive commandments. Every kohen who blesses is blessed from Heaven. In Baghdad they were careful to raise hands every day, and so it is fitting to practice in all congregations, for through Birkat Kohanim abundance is drawn down to the upper and lower worlds, and it contains deep secrets.
takeaways: A kohen who is fit to bless and refrains has nullified a positive commandment.
It is fitting to raise hands every day, as is the custom of Baghdad, since Birkat Kohanim draws down abundance.

paragraphs: The place where the kohanim stand to bless is on the platform (itztaba) next to the western wall which the congregation faces in prayer, for the meaning of "duchan" is "platform." And one who is lax in this, not going up onto the duchan to stand there, but instead standing on the floor of the sanctuary, is thereby deviating from the words of our Sages, for our Sages did not say for nothing that the kohanim should go up onto the duchan. And here in our city, may it be guarded, their custom was for the kohanim to stand on the floor of the sanctuary and bless Birkat Kohanim, and they did not stand on the platform at the rear of the sanctuary. And, praised be God, I instituted the custom that they go up and stand on the platform at the rear of the sanctuary, and bless there, and so it is fitting to be scrupulous about this in every place.

clarification.explanation: The place where the kohanim stand to bless is on the platform (a raised step) next to the wall which the congregation faces in prayer, for this is the meaning of "duchan." A kohen who is lax and does not go up onto the duchan, remaining on the floor of the sanctuary, deviates from the words of the Sages who required going up specifically onto the duchan. In Baghdad the kohanim used to stand on the floor of the sanctuary, and our teacher instituted that they go up and stand on the platform at the rear of the sanctuary and bless there, and so it is fitting to be scrupulous about this everywhere.
takeaways: The kohanim must go up and stand on the duchan (the raised platform), not on the floor.
Our teacher instituted this correction in Baghdad, and so it is fitting everywhere.

paragraphs: The kohanim shall not go up to the duchan wearing shoes, even if they are made of cloth, such as those worn on Yom Kippur; and some are stringent even regarding light house-slippers if they are made of leather.

clarification.explanation: The kohanim shall not go up to the duchan while wearing shoes, even shoes made of cloth, such as those worn on Yom Kippur. And some are stringent even regarding light house-slippers, if they are made of leather.
takeaways: One may not go up to the duchan wearing shoes, even if they are made of cloth.
Some are stringent even regarding light cloth slippers with a leather sole.

paragraphs: Even though the kohanim washed their hands in the morning, they wash again before Birkat Kohanim - a complete washing up to the joint that connects the hand and the forearm. And the Levite pours water on their hands, and before that the Levite washes his own hands. And if there is no Levite present, a firstborn from his mother's womb (peter rechem) pours for them; and if there is no firstborn present, they wash by themselves, and not through an Israelite [non-kohen, non-Levite]. And some say that if the Levite is a Torah scholar, he may not pour water on the hands of the kohanim, even if some of them are Torah scholars and some are unlearned - and certainly if all of them are unlearned, and one is liable to death by the hand of Heaven if he pours water on the hand of an unlearned kohen. And although there are those who permit this, one should be concerned [for the stringent view], and it is better to refrain from acting, even if there is no Levite present other than himself.

clarification.explanation: Even though the kohanim washed their hands in the morning, they wash again before Birkat Kohanim - a complete washing up to the joint (where the hand meets the forearm). The Levite pours water on their hands, and beforehand the Levite washes his own hands. If there is no Levite, a firstborn son (from his mother's womb) pours for them; and if there is no firstborn, they wash by themselves and not through an Israelite. Some say that if the Levite is a Torah scholar, he may not pour for an unlearned kohen, and there is great stringency in this matter. And since there is a dispute about it, it is preferable to refrain (sit and do not act), even when there is no other Levite available.
takeaways: The kohanim wash their hands again before the blessing, up to the forearm joint, and the Levite pours for them.
Order of priority for who pours: a Levite; if none, a firstborn; and if neither, the kohanim themselves.

paragraphs: Every God-fearing kohen should guard his hands from the time of his morning washing, so as not to touch the covered parts of his body; for if he touched them, there is a doubt as to whether he must wash and bless again when he washes his hands for Birkat Kohanim. And some say that pure water is required, which has not changed from its natural state, and that human effort (in the pouring) is also required, as in the law of washing hands [for bread]. And know that the blessing must be said immediately after the washing; therefore, where possible, he should be careful not to delay more than the time it takes to walk twenty-two amot (cubits) between the washing and Birkat Kohanim.

clarification.explanation: Every God-fearing kohen should guard his hands from the time of his morning washing, so as not to touch the covered parts of his body, for if he touched them there is a doubt whether he must wash and bless again before Birkat Kohanim. Some say pure water is required, which has not changed in appearance, and human effort in the pouring, as in the law of washing hands [before bread]. And the blessing must be adjacent to the washing; therefore, when possible, he should be careful not to delay between the washing and Birkat Kohanim more than the time it takes to walk twenty-two amot.
takeaways: A kohen should guard his hands from touching covered body parts after the morning washing.
The blessing must be adjacent to the washing, without a delay of more than twenty-two amot's walk.

paragraphs: When the prayer leader begins "Retzeh," every kohen in the synagogue must uproot himself from his place to go up to the duchan, even a kohen who is already standing in the sanctuary where he performs the raising of hands - he too must uproot his feet at "Retzeh." And if he did not uproot his feet before the prayer leader finished "Retzeh," he may not go up to the duchan; and if he uprooted his feet after the prayer leader finished "Retzeh," even if he went up, he must come down. And uprooting oneself from one's house in order to come to the synagogue is not considered an "uprooting" for the purpose of Birkat Kohanim; therefore, if he arrived at the synagogue after the prayer leader finished "Retzeh," he may not go up to the duchan - unless the uprooting from his house was with the intention of going up to the duchan, in which case he may go up even if he arrived at the synagogue after the prayer leader finished "Retzeh." And I wrote in a responsum in my holy books, Rav Pe'alim, that the conclusion of "Retzeh" is when he says "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTziyon" (Who restores His Presence to Zion), for up to that point it is called the blessing of Avodah (Divine service), but from "Modim, etc." onward it is the blessing of Hoda'ah (thanksgiving).

clarification.explanation: When the chazzan begins the blessing "Retzeh," every kohen in the synagogue must uproot his feet from his place to go up to the duchan, even a kohen who is already standing in the sanctuary. If he did not uproot his feet before the chazzan finished "Retzeh," he may not go up; and if he uprooted them after the chazzan finished "Retzeh," even if he went up he must come down. Uprooting one's feet from home to come to the synagogue is not considered an uprooting for this purpose, so one who arrives at the synagogue after the chazzan finished "Retzeh" may not go up - unless he left his house with the intention of going up to the duchan. And the conclusion of "Retzeh" is at the words "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTziyon," up to which point it is the blessing of Divine service.
takeaways: The kohen must uproot his feet to go up at the time of "Retzeh," before the chazzan finishes it.
The conclusion of "Retzeh" is at "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTziyon"; one who is late may not go up.

paragraphs: A congregation that was praying and had among them eight Israelites and three kohanim, and two of these three kohanim do not wish to perform the raising of hands for some reason, and wish to leave the synagogue - if the two leave, only nine will remain in the synagogue, namely eight Israelites and one kohen - how should they proceed? I addressed this in a responsum in my holy books, Rav Pe'alim, with the help of Heaven: They must leave before the prayer leader begins "Retzeh," and remain outside until the prayer leader concludes "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTziyon"; and when he begins the blessing of "Modim," they should enter the synagogue to complete the minyan (quorum). And the kohen who remained in the synagogue, who uprooted his feet at "Retzeh," performs the raising of hands alone, while the two others do not raise their hands, since they entered after the blessing of "Modim" and did not uproot their feet at "Retzeh." And regarding what our teacher Rabbi Isserlein of blessed memory wrote, quoted in the Shulchan Aruch, siman 128, that kohanim who leave observe a refinement of not re-entering until the kohanim in the synagogue finish Birkat Kohanim, so that people should not say of them that they are blemished - this applies where the congregation in the synagogue does not need them to complete the minyan; therefore, as the most proper practice, they observe this refinement. But in a case such as this, where they are needed to complete the minyan, such that if they do not enter before the blessing the mitzvah of the raising of hands would be nullified [for the whole congregation], one does not nullify the raising of hands for the congregation for the sake of this refinement that the kohanim practice. However, in such a case, certainly the prayer leader does not call out "Kohanim."

clarification.explanation: The case: a congregation praying that includes eight Israelites and three kohanim, and two of the kohanim do not wish to raise their hands and wish to leave, and if they leave no minyan will remain. What should they do? They should leave before the chazzan begins "Retzeh," and remain outside until the chazzan concludes "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTziyon," and when he begins "Modim" they should enter to complete the minyan. The kohen who remained and uprooted his feet at "Retzeh" raises his hands alone, and the two others do not raise theirs, since they entered after "Modim" and did not uproot their feet at "Retzeh." And since they are needed to complete the minyan, the raising of hands is not nullified because of them - except that in such a case the chazzan does not call out "Kohanim."
takeaways: Kohanim who will not raise their hands should leave before "Retzeh" and return at "Modim" to complete the minyan.
The kohen who remained blesses alone, and the chazzan does not call out "Kohanim."

paragraphs: If the prayer leader began the repetition of the Amidah with ten present, and some of them left before Birkat Kohanim, so that ten no longer remained - the prayer leader shall say "Our God and God of our fathers, bless us with the three-fold blessing," for this blessing belongs to the prayer [itself], and since he began with ten, he completes this blessing as well, as Olat Tamid, Shayarei Kenesset HaGedolah, and Eliyahu Rabbah wrote, and as I too concluded, with the help of Heaven, in my holy books, Rav Pe'alim.

clarification.explanation: If the chazzan began the repetition of the prayer with ten present, and afterward people left so that ten no longer remained before Birkat Kohanim, the chazzan shall say "Our God and God of our fathers, bless us with the three-fold blessing," for this blessing belongs to the prayer itself, and since he began with ten, he completes this blessing as well.
takeaways: The chazzan began the repetition with ten, and the minyan diminished before Birkat Kohanim.
He completes it and says "bless us with the three-fold blessing," since it is part of the prayer.

paragraphs: When the kohen uproots his feet to raise his hands, he should say: "For the sake of the union of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, etc. - behold I am ready and prepared to fulfill the positive commandment of blessing Israel with Birkat Kohanim through the raising of hands, to bring satisfaction to our Creator and to draw down abundance and blessing to all the worlds, etc." And when the kohanim stand on the duchan, after they have answered "Modim DeRabbanan," they say: "May it be Your will, our God and God of our fathers, that this blessing which You commanded us to bless Your people Israel be a complete blessing, without stumbling or iniquity, from now and forever." And they prolong this prayer until the prayer leader concludes "U'lecha na'eh lehodot" (and to You it is fitting to give thanks), so that the congregation's answer of amen will apply to both this and that.

clarification.explanation: When the kohen uproots his feet to raise his hands, he says a short "leshem yichud" formula, [stating] that he is ready and prepared to fulfill the commandment of Birkat Kohanim through the raising of hands, to bring satisfaction to his Creator and to draw down abundance and blessing to all the worlds. And when the kohanim stand on the duchan, after answering "Modim DeRabbanan," they recite a request that this blessing be a complete blessing without stumbling or iniquity, and they prolong this request until the chazzan concludes "U'lecha na'eh lehodot," so that the congregation's amen will rise upon both the chazzan's blessing and their own request.
takeaways: The kohen recites "leshem yichud" as he uproots his feet, along with a request that the blessing be complete.
He prolongs the request until "U'lecha na'eh lehodot," so that the amen applies to both.

paragraphs: The raising of hands does not require a place that contains a Torah scroll; rather, in any place where people pray, there is a raising of hands. And when they go up to the duchan, they stand facing the Ark. And if there are two or more kohanim, the chazzan calls out to them "Kohanim"; but if there is only one kohen, he does not call out to him - rather, he alone begins the blessing.

clarification.explanation: The raising of hands need not take place specifically in a location that has a Torah scroll; rather, in any place where people pray, there is a raising of hands. When they go up to the duchan they stand facing the Ark. If there are two or more kohanim, the chazzan calls out to them "Kohanim"; but if there is only a single kohen, he is not called out to - rather, he begins the blessing on his own.
takeaways: The raising of hands takes place in any place of prayer, even without a Torah scroll.
For two kohanim or more, the chazzan calls out "Kohanim"; for a single kohen he does not, and the kohen begins on his own.

paragraphs: They should raise their hands above their shoulders, so that their hands are exactly level with their heads, as written in Sha'ar HaKavanot; see also Torat Chacham, page 153, column 2, and page 154, column 1, on this matter. And they raise the right hand slightly above the left, in order to strengthen the attribute of mercy over the attribute of judgment. And they spread out their hands and separate their fingers to make five openings: between each pair of fingers, one opening; between the [index] finger and the thumb, [one opening]; and between the two thumbs, [one opening]; and the palms of their hands face the ground, and the backs of their hands face the heavens - all this according to what Maran of blessed memory wrote in his pure Shulchan Aruch. But in the holy Zohar, Parashat Naso, page 146, it is written that the fingers should not be joined to one another, so that the two holy crowns (kotarin) are each blessed separately, on its own. And Mikdash Melech writes that this is the opposite of the Shulchan Aruch, for here it says that all the fingers should be separated from one another; and so writes Aspaklarya HaMe'irah on the holy Zohar. And I asked the great sage, the pious one, our teacher Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may his light shine, to inform me of the custom of the chassidim of Beit El, may it be guarded, in Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt; and he wrote to me: In this matter there is no clear ruling - some do as the holy Zohar wrote, and some do as Maran of blessed memory wrote, and in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, nothing explicit is found on this matter. And here in our city, may it be guarded, they practice making five openings, though some practice according to the holy Zohar. And I further asked him to inform me of the custom of the chassidim of Beit El, may it be guarded, whether the kohanim's fingers are held upright as in the washing of hands, and he replied that here too there is no clear distinction - some do it this way and some do it that way.

clarification.explanation: The kohanim raise their hands above their shoulders, exactly level with their heads, and raise the right hand slightly above the left in order to strengthen mercy over judgment. They spread their hands and separate their fingers into five airy gaps (one gap between each pair of fingers, one between the finger and thumb, and one between the two thumbs), with the palms facing the ground and the backs of the hands facing the heavens, following Maran's view. But the Zohar states that the fingers should not touch one another at all, so that each finger stands independently - a departure from the words of the Shulchan Aruch. Rabbi Eliyahu Mani testified that there is no decisive custom on this in Beit El: some follow the Zohar and some follow Maran; in Baghdad the practice was to make five gaps, with some following the Zohar. And likewise, whether the fingers should be held upright, there is no clear ruling either.
takeaways: The hands are raised level with the head, with the right hand slightly above the left to strengthen mercy.
There is a dispute between the Shulchan Aruch (five gaps) and the Zohar (each finger separate); in Baghdad the practice follows Maran.

paragraphs: When the Divine Name is mentioned during Birkat Kohanim, the congregation answers "Baruch Hu U'varuch Shemo" (Blessed is He and blessed is His Name), as mentioned by the halachic authorities. And although there are those who do not hold this way, the widespread custom is to answer so, and so is the widespread custom in the holy city [Jerusalem], may it be rebuilt and established, and one should not deviate from it. And after the conclusion of each verse, the congregation answers amen, and they do not answer amen until the blessing is finished from the mouths of the kohanim. But the chazzan does not answer amen after the kohanim's blessing, and even after the blessing "to bless His people Israel with love," the chazzan shall not answer amen - even though he is assured that he will not become confused [in his prayer].

clarification.explanation: When the kohanim mention the Name of God in the blessing, the congregation answers "Baruch Hu U'varuch Shemo," and this is the widespread custom, not to be changed. After the conclusion of each verse the congregation answers "amen," and they do not answer until the blessing is finished from the mouths of the kohanim. But the chazzan does not answer amen after the kohanim's blessing at all, and even after "to bless His people Israel with love" he shall not answer, even if he is assured he would not become confused in his prayer.
takeaways: The congregation answers "Baruch Hu U'varuch Shemo" at the mention of the Name, and "amen" at the end of each verse.
The chazzan does not answer amen after the kohanim's blessing at all.

paragraphs: When they go up to the duchan, their faces shall be toward the Ark and their backs toward the people. And while their backs are toward the people, they begin the blessing "Who has sanctified us with the sanctity of Aaron and commanded us to bless His people Israel." They turn their faces toward the people and conclude with "be'ahavah" (with love), so that the conclusion of the blessing faces the people. And when the prayer leader begins "Sim Shalom," they then turn their faces toward the Ark, and not before; and then they say: "Master of the worlds, we have done what You decreed upon us; do You [now] what You have promised us: look forth from Your holy abode, from heaven, and bless Your people Israel" - and they do not complete this verse [in full]. And so is the custom in the holy city, may it be rebuilt and established speedily, to say up to this point and not complete the verse, and to prolong this prayer until the prayer leader concludes "Sim Shalom," so that the congregation will answer amen upon both. And on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, when [the chazzan] prolongs [the prayer], they should not begin saying "Ribon" until the end, so that they conclude together with the congregation. And the kohanim are not permitted to turn their faces back until the prayer leader begins "Sim Shalom," and they are not permitted to bend their fingers until they have turned their faces back, and they are not permitted to leave that place until the congregation has answered amen after the blessing "Sim Shalom." And whenever they turn their faces, whether at the beginning or at the end, they shall turn only by way of the right.

clarification.explanation: When they go up to the duchan their faces are toward the Ark and their backs toward the people. While their backs are to the people, they begin the blessing "Who has sanctified us with the sanctity of Aaron and commanded us to bless His people Israel," and at the word "be'ahavah" they turn their faces toward the people, so that the conclusion of the blessing faces the people. When the chazzan begins "Sim Shalom" they turn their faces toward the Ark, and not before, and then say the request "Master of the worlds, we have done what You decreed upon us; do You [now] what You have promised us," up to "and bless Your people Israel," without completing the verse, and they prolong it until the chazzan concludes "Sim Shalom," so that the congregation answers amen upon both. On Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, when it is prolonged, they should not begin "Ribon" until the end, so as to conclude together with the congregation. The kohanim may not turn their faces back until the chazzan begins "Sim Shalom"; they may not bend their fingers until after turning their faces back; and they may not leave their place until the congregation answers amen after the blessing "Sim Shalom." And every turning of the face shall be by way of the right.
takeaways: They open the blessing with their backs to the people, and turn to face the people at "be'ahavah."

At "Sim Shalom" they face the Ark and say "Ribon HaOlamim"; they bend their fingers only after turning back, and do not step down from the duchan until the congregation answers amen after "Sim Shalom"; every turn is made to the right.

paragraphs: The prayer leader does not call out "Kohanim" until the congregation's amen for the blessing "na'eh lehodot" has ended. And the kohanim are not permitted to begin the blessing "Who has sanctified us" until the words of the calling of "Kohanim" have ended from the mouth of the one calling. And they are not permitted to begin "yevarechecha" until the amen from the entire congregation after "be'ahavah" has ended. And they are not permitted to begin any word of Birkat Kohanim until the [previous] word has been completed by the one calling it out, and the congregation does not answer amen until the blessing has been completed from the mouths of the kohanim.

clarification.explanation: The chazzan does not call out "Kohanim" until the congregation's answer of "amen" to the blessing "U'lecha na'eh lehodot" has finished. The kohanim may not begin "Who has sanctified us" until the chazzan's calling of "Kohanim" has finished, and they do not begin "yevarechecha" until the entire congregation's "amen" after "be'ahavah" has finished. And regarding every word: the kohanim do not begin a word until the caller has finished it, and the congregation does not answer "amen" until the blessing has finished from the mouths of the kohanim.
takeaways: The order must be kept: each stage begins only after the previous one has fully ended.
The kohanim do not get ahead of the one calling out, and the congregation does not get ahead of the kohanim.

paragraphs: It is proper to make an effort that a kohen should not be the prayer leader for Shacharit and Musaf. And if the prayer leader was a kohen, if there are other kohanim present, he shall not raise his hands. And if there is no kohen there other than him, and he is assured that he will return to his own prayer without confusion of mind, then he does raise his hands, so that the raising of hands should not be omitted from that prayer. How shall he proceed? He shall uproot his feet at [the blessing of] Avodah, and say [the prayer] up to "U'lecha na'eh lehodot," and go up to the duchan and bless Birkat Kohanim; and if the entire congregation is ahead of him [in that section of the prayer], he shall bless them in his place, and someone else shall call out for him the calling of "Kohanim," and afterward he shall conclude with "Sim Shalom." And in every case where there are other kohanim present, such that we say the prayer leader should not raise his hands, he must stand in his place and remain silent, and another person shall stand beside him and call out to the kohanim, while the prayer leader remains silent until the beginning of "Sim Shalom."

clarification.explanation: It is proper to make an effort that the chazzan for Shacharit and Musaf not be a kohen. If the chazzan was a kohen and there are other kohanim present, he shall not raise his hands. And if there is no other kohen present besides him, and he is assured he will return to his prayer without becoming confused, he does raise his hands so that the blessing not be omitted: he uproots his feet at [the blessing of] "Retzeh"/Avodah, says [the prayer] up to "U'lecha na'eh lehodot," goes up to the duchan and blesses; and if the whole congregation is ahead of him he blesses in his place, and someone else calls out the blessing for him, after which he concludes "Sim Shalom." And wherever there are other kohanim present and the chazzan should not raise his hands, he stands in his place and remains silent, while another person stands beside him and calls out to the kohanim, and the chazzan remains silent until the beginning of "Sim Shalom."
takeaways: It is preferable that the chazzan not be a kohen; and if there are other kohanim present, the chazzan does not raise his hands.
If there is no other kohen, the chazzan does raise his hands, provided he is assured he will return to his prayer without becoming confused.

paragraphs: At the time the kohanim bless the people, the faces of the people shall be toward the kohanim, and they shall not look at the kohanim or at anything else; their eyes shall be closed, and they shall not let their minds wander to other matters, but shall be as though standing in prayer, and shall have intent for the blessing. And people who are behind the kohanim are not included in the blessing; and likewise those standing to the sides, as long as they do not stand within the space directly in front of the kohanim and onward, are not included in the blessing. But those standing to the sides of the space that is in front of them are included in the blessing, for it is not required that they be exactly in front of them, but rather this is [required] only as the most proper practice, where possible, as mentioned in Chesed LeAlafim. And if someone enters the synagogue to request something, or is a traveler passing from place to place, and finds the kohanim blessing Birkat Kohanim, he shall stand and listen to Birkat Kohanim and not leave until they have concluded Birkat Kohanim. And if he is a kohen and has already raised his hands that day, and comes to this synagogue and finds a congregation that has not yet reached Birkat Kohanim, he may raise his hands again.

clarification.explanation: At the time the kohanim bless, the faces of the people must be toward the kohanim, and they shall not look at the kohanim or at anything else, but shall stand with their eyes closed with intent, as in prayer. Those standing behind the kohanim are not included in the blessing, nor those standing to the sides who are not within the space in front of the kohanim; but those standing to the sides of the space in front of them are included in the blessing, since it is not required that they stand exactly opposite them. Someone who enters the synagogue for some purpose, or a traveler passing through, who finds the kohanim blessing, shall stand and listen and not leave until they finish. And a kohen who has already raised his hands that day and comes to another synagogue and finds a congregation that has not yet reached Birkat Kohanim may raise his hands again.
takeaways: The congregation stands facing the kohanim with closed eyes and intent, without looking at them.
Those standing behind are not included in the blessing; a kohen may raise his hands again in another synagogue.

paragraphs: A kohen who has not yet prayed and finds a congregation praying: if the time [for prayer] is not passing, he raises his hands, and the prayer does not hold him back; and if they told him "go up," he must go up even if the time is passing for him, for the raising of hands is [a commandment] from the Torah, while [the time-bound obligation of] prayer is rabbinic.

clarification.explanation: A kohen who has not yet prayed and finds a congregation praying: if the time [for prayer] is not passing, he raises his hands, and his prayer does not hold him back. And if they told him "go up," he must go up even if the time is passing for him, since the raising of hands is from the Torah while prayer is rabbinic.
takeaways: A kohen who has not yet prayed raises his hands if the time is not passing.
If he is told "go up," he must, since the raising of hands is a Torah commandment while prayer is rabbinic.

paragraphs: A kohen who is reciting the Shema and senses that the prayer leader is about to reach Birkat Kohanim shall hasten to finish the Shema, reciting it even while walking to go up, so that he finishes it before he begins to bless. And if he sensed this while still in the blessings of the Shema, he shall wait there at a break between the sections and not begin the Shema itself until he has blessed Birkat Kohanim. And if he did not sense it until the prayer leader began "Retzeh," and he had already begun the Shema, and he is slow of speech such that it is not possible for him to hurry to finish the Shema before blessing - he shall uproot his feet at [the blessing of] Avodah, finish the passage he is in the midst of, and bless Birkat Kohanim between the sections of the Shema, and after Birkat Kohanim he shall finish the Shema. But if he did not sense it during Avodah, and did not uproot his feet before the prayer leader finished the blessing of Avodah, he does not go up to the duchan to bless - as I have written above, that anyone who did not uproot his feet during Avodah does not go up to the duchan, as I concluded, with the help of Heaven, in my holy books, Rav Pe'alim. And if the kohen is standing in the [silent] Amidah, I wrote there in my holy books, Rav Pe'alim, that even according to the view of the Magen Avraham and those who agree with him, who hold that he interrupts [his prayer to go up], this is only if he was told to go up, and he must be told this when the prayer leader says "Retzeh." But in truth there are those who disagree with the Magen Avraham and hold that he does not interrupt if he is standing in the Amidah, as in the law of Kaddish and Kedushah. And even according to the view of those who hold that if the praying kohen concluded "U'lecha na'eh lehodot" he then raises his hands there [where he stands], nevertheless, since he did not uproot his foot during Avodah, he does not go up. And certainly he did not uproot his feet, since he was occupied with his own prayer, and certainly they would not tell him to go up, since they see him occupied in prayer; and since they did not tell him to go up, then even according to the view of Rabbi Meir Mintz, siman 12, he does not raise his hands.

clarification.explanation: A kohen reciting the Shema who senses that the chazzan is close to Birkat Kohanim shall hurry to finish the Shema, even while walking up, in order to finish before the blessing. If he sensed this while still in the blessings surrounding the Shema, he shall wait at a break between the sections and not begin the Shema itself until after he has blessed Birkat Kohanim. And if he did not sense it until "Retzeh" and had already begun the Shema, and is slow of speech so that he cannot hurry to finish before the blessing - he shall uproot his feet at "Retzeh," finish the passage he is in, and bless between the sections of the Shema, and afterward finish the Shema. But if he did not uproot his feet before the chazzan finished the blessing of "Avodah," he does not go up to the duchan at all. And a kohen standing in the [silent] Amidah itself does not go up unless he was explicitly told to go up at the time of "Retzeh" - and in practice there are those who disagree even with that, and since he did not uproot his feet during Avodah, he does not go up.
takeaways: A kohen reciting the Shema should hurry or wait between sections in order to bless at the proper point.
The principle: whoever did not uproot his feet at "Retzeh" does not go up to the duchan.

paragraphs: A kohen who is a mourner leaves the synagogue at the time [the chazzan] calls "Kohanim," and after the seven days of mourning he raises his hands. And some say that even during the seven days he raises his hands, and a good blessing will come upon him. And in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and established, the custom is to perform the raising of hands in the house of mourning, and so it has newly become the custom here in our city of Baghdad, may it be guarded; only the mourning kohanim themselves did not practice raising their hands, and one must warn them not to stand there, but rather to go, before "Retzeh," into another room in the house. See Shalmei Tzibbur, and see what the glossator wrote in Chesed LeAlafim in the name of Rabbi Chaim Pinso of blessed memory - see there. And the congregation of chassidim of Beit El, may it be guarded, practice performing the raising of hands on the ninth of Av at Shacharit, but here in our city, may it be guarded, they did not practice this at Shacharit on the ninth of Av; rather, only at Mincha do they perform the raising of hands, and I did not change their custom in this regarding the ninth of Av, for a reason hidden within me.

clarification.explanation: A mourning kohen leaves the synagogue at the time "Kohanim" is called, and after the seven days of mourning he raises his hands; and some say that even during the seven days he raises his hands, to his blessing. In Jerusalem the custom is to perform the raising of hands in the house of mourning, and this has become the new custom in Baghdad as well - except that the mourning kohanim themselves did not raise their hands, and one must warn them not to stand there but to enter another room before "Retzeh." In Beit El they practice raising hands on the ninth of Av at Shacharit, but in Baghdad they did not practice this at Shacharit, only at Mincha of the ninth of Av, and our teacher did not change their custom in this matter for a reason kept within him.
takeaways: A mourning kohen does not raise his hands during the seven days, and leaves at the time of the calling.
In Baghdad they raise hands on the ninth of Av only at Mincha, not at Shacharit.

paragraphs: The raising of hands is not performed at Mincha, except on a public fast day, when it is customary to pray late, such as the time of the Ne'ilah prayer of Yom Kippur. And in my responsum in my holy books, Rav Pe'alim, I concluded that they should be instructed, as the preferred practice, to perform the raising of hands on a public fast day forty minutes before the calling of "HaMa'arav" (the evening prayer), which is half an hour before sunset; for here in our city the sun sets ten minutes before the calling of "HaMa'arav." However, those who perform it before the aforementioned time should not be protested against, for they have upon what to rely.

clarification.explanation: The raising of hands is not performed at Mincha, except on a public fast day when it is customary to pray late, at a time similar to the Ne'ilah prayer of Yom Kippur. Our teacher ruled that as the preferred practice, the raising of hands should be performed on a public fast day about forty minutes before the calling of the evening prayer - a point that is about half an hour before sunset, since in Baghdad the sun sets about ten minutes before that calling. Those who perform it somewhat before this measure should not be protested against, since they have grounds to rely on.
takeaways: The raising of hands at Mincha occurs only on a public fast day, at the late hour similar to Ne'ilah.
The proper time: about half an hour before sunset (in Baghdad, about forty minutes before the calling of the evening prayer).

paragraphs: These halachot pertain to Purim; my practice is to expound them, with the help of Heaven, on Shabbat Zachor, which for the most part occurs at the time of Parashat Tetzaveh, and their connection [to the parasha] shall be made within the sermon as it happens to fall each and every year, with the help of Heaven.

clarification.explanation: These halachot pertain to Purim, and our teacher's practice was to expound them on Shabbat Zachor, which for the most part falls at the time of Parashat Tetzaveh, and their connection to the parasha is made within the sermon as it happens to occur each year.
takeaways: The halachot of Purim are expounded on Shabbat Zachor, which usually falls at the time of Parashat Tetzaveh.

paragraphs: All are obligated in the reading of the Megillah, men and women; but women, even though they know how to read, shall listen from the men. And so is the custom in the holy city, may it be rebuilt and established, that it has never been heard that a woman read the Megillah [for others]. Therefore, every man, even though he has read the Megillah in the synagogue, shall read it again in his home for his wife, who did not hear it in the synagogue, and for the unmarried girls and the other women and servants of the household. And if he read it and then reads again for the women, he shall not make the blessing on their behalf, nor shall they make the blessing themselves.

clarification.explanation: All are obligated in the reading of the Megillah, men and women. But the women, even though they know how to read, shall listen from the men, and so is the custom - it has never been heard that a woman read the Megillah. Therefore, every man, even though he read the Megillah in the synagogue, shall read it again at home for his wife who did not hear it in the synagogue, and for the unmarried girls, the other women, and the household servants. And if he already read in the synagogue and reads again for the women, he shall not make the blessing on their behalf, nor shall they make the blessing themselves.
takeaways: Women are obligated in the Megillah but hear it from the men and do not read it themselves.
One who reads again at home for the women after having heard it in the synagogue does not make the blessing.

paragraphs: If the reader was deaf-mute, mentally incompetent, or a minor, one who hears from him has not fulfilled his obligation, and must go back and read it again with the blessing. However, if she heard it from a deaf-mute [who can speak but not hear], she shall go back and read it again without a blessing, since there are those who hold that one who hears from a deaf-mute [in this sense] has fulfilled the obligation. And if she heard it from a minor who has reached the age of [religious] training, she shall go back and read it again without a blessing, since there are many who hold that a minor who has reached the age of training can fulfill the obligation for an adult. And likewise, if she heard it from a woman, she shall go back and read it again without a blessing.

clarification.explanation: If the reader was deaf-mute [in the sense of one lacking full faculties], mentally incompetent, or a minor [who has not reached the age of training], one who hears from him has not fulfilled the obligation at all and must go back and read with a blessing. But if one heard from a person who can speak but not hear, he shall go back and read without a blessing, since some hold that hearing from such a person fulfills the obligation. Likewise, if one heard from a minor who has reached the age of training, he shall go back and read without a blessing, since many hold that such a minor can fulfill the obligation even for an adult. And likewise, if one heard from a woman, he shall go back and read without a blessing.
takeaways: One who hears from someone mentally incompetent, or a minor below the age of training, has not fulfilled the obligation at all and reads again with a blessing; one who hears from a person who can speak but not hear, from a minor who has reached the age of training, or from a woman, reads again without a blessing, out of doubt.
Out of doubt, one does not bless again, since there are lenient views in all these cases.

paragraphs: One who read [the Megillah] while drowsy, since he did not fall into a deep sleep, has fulfilled the obligation. But one who listens while drowsy has not fulfilled the obligation, and one must be careful about this matter, which is quite common, that these listeners tend to become drowsy. And as the preferred practice, if they saw the reader reading some verses while drowsy, they should require him to go back and read it again, for we only say that one who read it while drowsy has fulfilled the obligation after the fact, in a case where he completed the reading of the entire Megillah.

clarification.explanation: One who read the Megillah while drowsy, since he did not fall into a deep sleep, has fulfilled the obligation. But one who listens while drowsy has not fulfilled the obligation, and one must be careful about this, since it commonly happens that listeners become drowsy. As the preferred practice, if it was observed that the reader read some verses while drowsy, he is required to go back and read it again, since the ruling that one who read while drowsy has fulfilled the obligation applies only after the fact, once he has completed reading the entire Megillah.
takeaways: A drowsy reader has fulfilled the obligation after the fact, but a drowsy listener has not.
As the preferred practice, a reader who dozed off partway through is required to start over.

paragraphs: One who reads the Megillah must make the blessings while standing, both at the beginning and at the end, even if he is reading it alone in his own home; but the reading itself does not require standing, and only the prayer leader reads it standing, out of respect for the congregation. And he must unroll the entire Megillah [before blessing] and afterward make the blessings while standing; however, since he unrolls it and blesses while standing, he must have before him a table or chair on which the Megillah can rest, so that it does not drag on the ground.

clarification.explanation: One who reads the Megillah makes the blessings while standing, at the beginning and at the end, even if reading it alone at home. But the reading itself does not require standing, and only the prayer leader reads it standing, out of respect for the congregation. He must unroll the entire Megillah before the blessing, and since he unrolls it and blesses while standing, he must have before him a table or chair for the Megillah to rest on, so that it does not drag on the ground.
takeaways: The blessings on the Megillah are made standing, at the beginning and the end, even by an individual.
The entire Megillah is unrolled before the blessing, and rested on a table so it does not drag on the ground.

paragraphs: One who forgot and did not recite the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" - if he remembers after he has begun [reading], he shall recite it at the point where he remembers. And in my holy book Makabtziel, I concluded that if he did not remember until after he has already read the verse of the ten sons of Haman, even though he has not yet finished the Megillah, he shall not recite "Shehecheyanu" at that point where he remembers.

clarification.explanation: One who forgot to recite the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" before the reading, if he remembers after having begun, shall recite it at the point where he remembers. But if he did not remember until after he has already read the verse of the ten sons of Haman, even though he has not yet finished the Megillah, he shall no longer recite "Shehecheyanu" there.
takeaways: One who forgot "Shehecheyanu" and remembers partway through the reading recites it at that point.
If he has passed the verse of the ten sons of Haman, he no longer recites it.

paragraphs: If the reader omitted words in his reading, even words that do not affect the meaning of the passage, he has not fulfilled the obligation. And one who has in his possession a Megillah that is not valid shall listen to the prayer leader and remain silent.

clarification.explanation: If the reader omitted words in his reading, even words that do not change the meaning of the matter, he has not fulfilled the obligation. And one who has an invalid Megillah in his possession shall not read from it, but shall listen to the chazzan and remain silent.
takeaways: Omitting words, even ones not essential to the meaning, invalidates the fulfillment of the obligation.
One without a valid Megillah listens to the chazzan and remains silent.

paragraphs: It is customary to say four verses of redemption aloud: "Ish Yehudi, etc.," "BaLailah HaHu, etc.," "U'Mordechai Yatza, etc.," and "LaYehudim Haytah Orah, etc." And when saying the verse "BaLailah HaHu" aloud with melody, one shall conclude the word "HaMelech" (the king) aloud and with extra melody. And some are accustomed to say aloud also the verse "Ki Mordechai HaYehudi, etc.," but here in our city they were not accustomed to do so with this verse.

clarification.explanation: It is customary to say four verses of redemption aloud: "Ish Yehudi," "BaLailah HaHu," "U'Mordechai Yatza," "LaYehudim Haytah Orah." And when saying "BaLailah HaHu" aloud with melody, one prolongs the word "HaMelech" in particular. Some are accustomed to also say the verse "Ki Mordechai HaYehudi" aloud, but in Baghdad they were not accustomed to do so with this verse.
takeaways: Four verses of redemption are said aloud, headed by "Ish Yehudi."
In "BaLailah HaHu" the word "HaMelech" is prolonged.

paragraphs: One must say, from the beginning of "Chamesh Me'ot Ish" and "Ve'et Parshandata, etc." through "Aseret," in a single breath, and prolong the vav of "VeVaizata." And the custom is to stamp with one's feet on the ground when saying the names of the ten sons of Haman; and some are accustomed to strike with their hands on the ground, but this is not a becoming custom - rather, it is proper to stamp with the sandals on one's feet.

clarification.explanation: The names of the ten sons of Haman, from "Chamesh Me'ot Ish" and "Ve'et Parshandata" through "Aseret," must be said in a single breath, and one prolongs the vav of "VeVaizata." The custom is to stamp with the feet on the floor when saying the names of the ten sons of Haman. Some are accustomed to strike with the hand on the floor, but this is not a becoming custom - rather it is proper to stamp with the sandals on one's feet.
takeaways: The names of the ten sons of Haman are said in a single breath, with a prolongation of the vav of "VeVaizata."
One stamps with the feet (in sandals), not with the hand.

paragraphs: One must be careful to read the word "ve'et" mentioned [before each of] the ten sons of Haman directly from the Megillah, for some err, out of haste, and read all the instances of the word "ve'et" mentioned from memory, in a single breath; therefore one must pay attention and be careful about this. And when saying "vayikar," he shall place his hands on his tefillin and kiss them; and when he says "the letter of Purim," he shall shake the Megillah at the word "iggeret" (letter).

clarification.explanation: One must be careful to read the words "ve'et" that appear before the ten sons of Haman directly from the Megillah itself, since some err, out of haste, and read all the instances of "ve'et" from memory; therefore one must pay attention to this. When saying "vayikar," one places his hands on the tefillin and kisses them, and when saying "the letter of Purim," one shakes the Megillah at the word "iggeret" (letter).
takeaways: The words "ve'et" are read from the text, not from memory.
Customs: kissing the tefillin at "vayikar," and shaking the Megillah at "iggeret."

paragraphs: The Gaon Ya'avetz, of blessed memory, wrote about his father the Gaon, of blessed memory, that he would stamp with his foot and strike with his sandal whenever he mentioned the name of Haman during the reading of the Megillah - see there. And I am accustomed to strike with my feet at the first mention of the name "Haman" written in the verse "After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hamedatha the Agagite," and also at the last mention of the name "Haman" in the verse "For Haman the son of Hamedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted, etc."

clarification.explanation: The Gaon Ya'avetz wrote of his father that he would stamp with his foot and strike with his sandal at every mention of the name "Haman" during the reading of the Megillah. Our teacher was accustomed to strike with his feet only at the first mention of "Haman," in the verse "After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hamedatha the Agagite," and at the last mention of "Haman," in the verse "For Haman the son of Hamedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted, etc."
takeaways: Some struck at every mention of the name "Haman."
Our teacher was accustomed to strike only at the first and the last mention of "Haman" in the Megillah.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to eat before the reading of the Megillah. And if a person has a valid Megillah from which he reads for himself in the synagogue while the prayer leader is reading it there for the congregation, and he does not wish to fulfill his obligation through the prayer leader's blessing but wishes to make the blessing for himself, he is permitted to do so; however, he shall make the blessing quietly, as I have concluded in my holy book Rav Pe'alim, with the help of Heaven.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to eat before the reading of the Megillah. And one who has a valid Megillah and reads it for himself in the synagogue while the chazzan is reading for the congregation, and does not wish to fulfill his obligation through the chazzan's blessing but wishes to bless for himself, is permitted to do so, but shall make the blessing quietly.
takeaways: It is forbidden to eat before the reading of the Megillah.
One who reads from his own Megillah may bless for himself, but quietly.

paragraphs: It is good that two people stand beside the prayer leader, on his right and on his left, and the prayer leader shall say before the blessing, "With the permission of my teachers and masters," and then bless and read. And the custom of our city is that the congregation stands during the blessing, at the beginning and at the end. And every person must roll up [the Megillah] and only afterward recite the concluding blessing, and he must be careful not to recite the blessing while he is rolling the Megillah.

clarification.explanation: It is good that two people stand beside the chazzan, to his right and to his left, and the chazzan says before the blessing, "With the permission of my teachers and masters," and then blesses and reads. The custom of Baghdad is that the congregation stands during the blessing, at the beginning and at the end. Every person rolls up the Megillah and only afterward recites the concluding blessing, and he must be careful not to recite the blessing while still rolling it.
takeaways: Two people stand beside the chazzan, and he opens with "With the permission of my teachers and masters."
One rolls up the Megillah before the concluding blessing, and does not bless while rolling it.

paragraphs: One who reads alone shall also recite the concluding blessing of the Megillah, as mentioned in Birkei Yosef; see also Machazik Bracha, siman 31, letter 108 - see there. And so is the custom here in our city, and so it is fitting to practice everywhere, and the individual should not lose out on this precious blessing.

clarification.explanation: One who reads the Megillah alone also recites the blessing that follows the Megillah, and so is the custom in Baghdad, and so it is fitting to practice everywhere, so that the individual not lose out on this precious blessing.
takeaways: Even one who reads alone recites the blessing that follows the Megillah.
It is fitting that the individual not forgo this blessing.

paragraphs: "Al HaNisim" is said in the prayer and in the Grace after Meals specifically on the fourteenth day, but not on the fifteenth. And even in a place where the Megillah is read on the fifteenth out of doubt as to whether it was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua, they nonetheless do not say "Al HaNisim" in the prayer or the Grace after Meals, out of concern for an improper interruption [in the prayer], as is explicitly stated in Sha'ar HaKavanot. And here in our city of Baghdad, may it be guarded, the custom is to read the Megillah on the fourteenth with a blessing, but on the fifteenth they read it without any blessing at all, and the concluding blessing is said without [mentioning] the Name and Sovereignty [of God]. And their custom is to read on the fifteenth from a Torah scroll the passage "Vayavo Amalek." And the reason is that the city of Baghdad is in doubt as to whether it was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua or not; therefore they read the Megillah on the fifteenth without a blessing. And formerly the custom here in our city was to say "Al HaNisim" on the fifteenth day as well, in the prayer and the Grace after Meals; but the great and honored sage, my grandfather, our teacher Rabbi Moshe Chaim, of blessed memory, abolished the custom of saying "Al HaNisim" out of concern for improper interruption, but he did not wish to abolish the Torah reading, since there is no concern of a wasted blessing in that. Therefore now they do not say "Al HaNisim" here in our city of Baghdad except on the fourteenth day alone. And if one forgot and did not say it, he is not required to go back, but rather in the prayer he says, after "Elohai Netzor," "We thank You, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, for the miracles," etc.; and in the Grace after Meals he says, after concluding the blessings, "May the Merciful One perform for us miracles as He performed for our fathers in those days, in this time, and in the days of Mordechai," etc.

Even in a place that reads the Megillah on the fifteenth out of doubt whether it was walled from the days of Joshua, they do not say "Al HaNisim" on the fifteenth out of concern for improper interruption in prayer. Formerly they also said "Al HaNisim" on the fifteenth, but our teacher's grandfather abolished this custom out of concern for interruption, though he did not abolish the Torah reading, since there is no concern of a wasted blessing there. One who forgot to say "Al HaNisim" is not required to repeat the prayer, but says it after "Elohai Netzor" in the Amidah, and in Grace after Meals in the "HaRachaman" formula.
takeaways: "Al HaNisim" is said only on the fourteenth, even in places that read on the fifteenth out of doubt.
In Baghdad the Megillah is read on the fifteenth without a blessing and from a Torah scroll, out of doubt whether the city was walled.

paragraphs: Every person is obligated to give two gifts to at least two poor people, and whoever gives more is praiseworthy. And the measure is: if he gives food, it must contain [the value of] three eggs, which is four or five dirhams; and if he gives money, the measure is enough to buy three eggs' worth of bread. And even a poor person who is supported by charity is obligated in gifts to the poor, though the Peri Chadash exempts him. And it is written in the book Torah LiShmah that one poor person may give to his fellow poor person, and this one in turn gives it again to his fellow.

And mishloach manot must be sent to an adult, but gifts to the poor fulfill the obligation even if given to a minor.

paragraphs: It is a mitzvah to abound in the festive meal of Purim, and the essential [obligation for the] meal is during the day; if one made it at night, he has not fulfilled the obligation. And it is a good custom to eat legumes on Purim, in remembrance of the eating of legumes by Daniel and his companions, for whom the Holy One, blessed be He, performed a miracle in this regard. Therefore here in our city the custom is to fry a pastry filled with legumes and meat together, which is called in Arabic "sambusak."
